summary: Depth-first rabbithole dossier for What-we-know / what-we-are-doing / next-update-at triple; source-anchored research pack.

facts.text: - **S01.** The triple is one incident status update made of three slots: what is known, what is being done, and when the next update will come. [M scope, H scope, P scope] - **S02.** No primary source found uses exactly the three labels "what we know / what we're doing / next update at". The name is practitioner shorthand for a shape that recurs across templates. [M note, H §Disagreements, H §Gaps] https://incident.io/blog/incident-communication-best-practices - **S03.** One search summary credited the triple to the PostHog handbook. The fetched page did not contain it, so no report cites that

In scope: when the three-part status update (what we know / what we are doing / next update at) breaks down, how it fails, where sources disagree about it, and evidence against it. Out of scope: sibling comms concepts (severity schemes, status-page tooling, postmortems, audience segmentation) and the wider Incident Comms domain.

- **Gate met.** The report uses at least 3 independent hosts: cdc.gov, sre.google, response.pagerduty.com / stakeholders.pagerduty.com, atlassian.com, docs.publishing.service.gov.uk, incident.io, openstatus.dev. I searched for disconfirming sources and found some (see the "Against" items above). - **Not found.** No primary source was found that coins the literal "what we know / what we're doing / next update at" label set. The literal triple appears to be practitioner shorthand distilled from the sources above. One search summary attributed the triple to the PostHog handbook, but the fetched p

- **Is a specific next-update time required?** - For: CDC Field Epi Manual (claim 6), Atlassian templates (claim 13), incident.io (claim 16). - Against: Atlassian's own DNS-provider template says only "We will update here as soon as we receive additional information from our provider." https://www.atlassian.com/dam/jcr:fc1c3565-32f8-47a5-ac3d-bbf594068037/incident_communication_templates.pdf - Against: GOV.UK's Statuspage guidance uses "We'll update this page as soon as we know what's causing it." https://docs.publishing.service.gov.uk/manual/post-a-statuspage-message.html - Against: the Mixpa

1. Slot 1, "what we know", states the current understanding of the problem and its impact. incident.io's internal template fills it with "Issue: [Brief description of the issue]" and "Root Cause: [What we found]". https://incident.io/blog/incident-communication-best-practices 2. Slot 2, "what we're doing", states the actions under way. incident.io's template labels it "Actions Taken: [What we're doing to resolve]". https://incident.io/blog/incident-communication-best-practices 3. Slot 3, "next update at", is a time commitment. incident.io labels it "Next update expected by: [time]". https://in

- **S07.** incident.io fills slot 1 with "Issue: [Brief description of the issue]" and "Root Cause: [What we found]". [M1] https://incident.io/blog/incident-communication-best-practices - **S08.** In the CERC form, slot 1 includes the unknowns. That makes it a statement of where knowledge stops, not only a list of facts. [M8, E1] https://www.cdc.gov/cerc/media/pdfs/CERC_Introduction.pdf - **S09.** CDC's Field Epidemiology Manual, chapter 12 (2024-08-08), says: "Explain what is currently known and unknown." [H7] https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/communicating-investigation.html

8. The next-update-at leg converts an open-ended wait into a finite one. Maister's "Uncertain Waits Are Longer than Known, Finite Waits" says a patient told of a 30-minute delay "relaxes into an acceptance", while one told "soon" stays in "nervous anticipation". https://www.columbia.edu/~ww2040/4615S13/Psychology_of_Waiting_Lines.pdf 9. The what-we-know and what-we're-doing legs apply Maister's "Unexplained Waits Are Longer than Explained Waits"; an explanation "may or may not exculpate the service provider, but is better than no explanation at all." https://www.columbia.edu/~ww2040/4615S13/Ps

5. openstatus (2026-08-15) says: "Never promise an ETA you are not certain of. A missed ETA converts a technical problem into a trust problem. Promise the *next update time* instead — that is entirely within your control." https://www.openstatus.dev/guides/incident-communication 6. openstatus counts an update with nothing new as complete: "Still investigating, no change, next update in 30 minutes." https://www.openstatus.dev/guides/incident-communication 7. PagerDuty's external guidelines say that each update should "provide an expectation of when the next update will be posted." https://respo

10. PagerDuty sets the heartbeat at "at least every 20 minutes" from the scoping update, for the first two hours only. After two hours it lets frequency drop, but an update is still required when impact "has meaningfully changed." https://response.pagerduty.com/during/external_communication_guidelines/ 11. PagerDuty's internal-liaison role uses a different cadence, "roughly every 30mins" to executives. So the internal and external clocks can run at different rates in the same incident. https://response.pagerduty.com/during/during_an_incident/ 12. openstatus sets the cadence by severity: SEV0/1

13. Atlassian Statuspage's "Investigating" templates follow the triple in order: state ("We are currently experiencing a service disruption"), action ("Our [ADD TEAM] team is working to identify the root cause and implement a solution"), next update ("We will send an additional update in [NEXT UPDATE TIME] minutes"). https://www.atlassian.com/dam/jcr:fc1c3565-32f8-47a5-ac3d-bbf594068037/incident_communication_templates.pdf 14. Atlassian's support-site template library uses the same "We will send an additional update in NEXT_UPDATE minutes" placeholder across several scenarios. https://support.

- **Commit to a next-update time or to a resolution ETA?** - Next-update time only, never an uncertain ETA: https://www.openstatus.dev/guides/incident-communication - Always state when the next update comes: https://response.pagerduty.com/during/external_communication_guidelines/ - Give "an estimated time to fix" once the cause is identified, with no next-update field: https://docs.publishing.service.gov.uk/manual/post-a-statuspage-message.html - State resolution windows cautiously ("we expect resolution within [timeframe]"): https://incident.io/blog/incident-communication-best-practices - **K

1. The triple is a practitioner compression of CDC's "Be Right" principle: "Information can include what is known, what is not known, and what is being done to fill in the gaps." (CERC Introduction, 2018 update, p.3) https://www.cdc.gov/cerc/media/pdfs/CERC_Introduction.pdf 2. CERC's initial-phase guidance adds the forward-looking leg: "Explain what your organization is doing to respond to the emergency and how you continue to provide updates." (p.7) https://www.cdc.gov/cerc/media/pdfs/CERC_Introduction.pdf 3. CERC lists "Information released late" as one of five pitfalls to avoid. (p.8) https

21. **Heartbeat not required.** NCSC NZ allows the first message to say that updates will follow only when significant developments occur. Under that rule no next-update time is promised. This contradicts the "post on schedule even with nothing new" rule in claims 6 and 17. https://www.ncsc.govt.nz/protect-your-organisation/public-communications-for-cyber-security-incidents-a-framework-for-organisations/ 22. **Stating uncertainty has a small cost.** Van der Bles et al. 1. The CDC CERC manual (2018 update) says that accurate information "can include what is known, what is not known, and what is being done to fill in the gaps." The incident-comms triple leaves out the middle item, "what is not known." https://www.cdc.gov/cerc/media/pdfs/CERC_Introduction.pdf 2. CERC's Maintenance phase warns: "When there are gaps in information, people may start to speculate." So an update that states only what we know, and not what we don't know, leaves the gaps for rumour to fill. https://www.cdc.gov/cerc/media/pdfs/CERC_Introduction.pdf 3. 8. Slot 1 in the CERC form explicitly includes unknowns ("what is not known"). So "what we know" is a statement of the knowledge boundary, not only a list of facts. https://www.cdc.gov/cerc/media/pdfs/CERC_Introduction.pdf 9. Slot 2 exists because silence is read as inaction. Google's SRE Workbook states: "Unless you acknowledge that an incident is happening and actively being addressed, people will automatically assume nothing is being done to resolve the issue." https://sre.google/workbook/incident-response/ 10. Slot 3 bounds the silence that follows the update. PagerDuty requires external u

21. A committed next-update time is itself an appointment. Maister: "an appointment defines an expectation that must be met", and waiting past the appointed time "has no knowable limit", so even a short overrun annoys. https://www.columbia.edu/~ww2040/4615S13/Psychology_of_Waiting_Lines.pdf 22. Maister also names the repeated-slip failure: a pilot who keeps announcing "only a few more minutes" makes the wait worse, and passengers feel "they are not being dealt with honestly". https://www.columbia.edu/~ww2040/4615S13/Psychology_of_Waiting_Lines.pdf 23. incident.io warns that broken update commi

Met. Nine independent hosts were used: cdc.gov, response.pagerduty.com, atlassian.com, support.atlassian.com, incident.io, docs.publishing.service.gov.uk, sre.google, columbia.edu (Maister) and phys.org/pnas.org (van der Bles et al. 2020). Primary or official sources: CDC CERC, PagerDuty's response docs, the Google SRE Workbook, GOV.UK and a peer-reviewed PNAS study. The search for disconfirming evidence found three things: Maister's appointment-syndrome risk (claim 21), Atlassian's event-conditional template, and GOV.UK's ETA guidance. Gaps: I found no empirical study that measures the triple

15. **The channel itself fails.** On 2017-02-28, AWS "were unable to update the individual services' status on the AWS Service Health Dashboard … because of a dependency the SHD administration console has on Amazon S3." Every next-update-at promise was unkeepable on that channel for the duration. https://aws.amazon.com/message/41926/ 16. **The update is not sent, or the incident is not closed.** The SRE Workbook says that without acknowledgement "people will automatically assume nothing is being done." It adds that if you forget to call off the response, "people will assume the incident is ong

14. PagerDuty cadence: updates "at least every 20 minutes from the scoping update during the first two hours". After that, the team may lower the frequency under a long-incident model, but it must "continue to provide expectations of when the next update will be posted". https://response.pagerduty.com/during/external_communication_guidelines/ 15. Atlassian Statuspage cadence: "Provide updates every 30 minutes (or whatever cadence is appropriate for the situation)." https://support.atlassian.com/statuspage/docs/incident-communication-tips/ 16. incident.io's "heartbeat" rule: update SEV1 inciden

- **S82.** No report found a controlled or peer-reviewed study of the triple itself. Its effect claims (S36, S67, S68) come from practitioner and vendor sources and from CERC doctrine. [M §Gaps, E23, P §Gaps] - **S83.** The only peer-reviewed evidence is van der Bles et al., PNAS 117(14):7672–7683, 2020-04-07: five experiments, n = 5,780, including a BBC News field test. It tested uncertainty in news facts, not incident updates, so applying it here is an extrapolation. [E22, P13] https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1913678117 https://research.rug.nl/en/publications/the-effects-of-communicati

Naming note: none of the sources below calls this a "triple". The name is a label for a pattern that appears in several templates and frameworks. The three-slot shape is consistent across them; the exact wording is not.
